findings.title: Every success criterion has a traceable task and test-with pattern is followed
findings.description: All 14 success criteria from the slice design are covered by named tasks with per-task success criteria a junior AI can check (see table above). Sequencing is correct: enum/field (1.1–1.2) → loader (1.3) → config tests (1.4) → enforcement module (2.1–2.2) → unit tests (2.3) → SimulationManager wiring (3.1–3.3) → integration tests (3.4–3.5) → config defaults (4.x) → final verification (5.x). Each section's test task immediately follows its implementation task, and each commit lands at a tested point. Task sizing fits the 2/5 effort slice; the two halves of Section 2 (dispatch skeleton + helpers) are small but each independently completable. No NFR is restated by the slice, so no load-test requirement applies; the slice's own "zero overhead on OPEN" note is appropriately satisfied by a cheap enum comparison plus a mock-based test rather than a benchmark.

findings.title: Commit markers are checkboxes rather than plain lines
findings.description: The five commit markers (lines 96, 179, 249, 286, 325) are written as `- [ ] **Commit:** ...` checkbox items, and commits are split out into dedicated tasks (1.5, 2.4, 3.6, 4.3, 5.5). The review convention is for `**Commit**:` markers to be plain lines at working, tested points, not checkbox tasks. This is a clash with the project's CLAUDE.md convention ("Use checklist format for all task files. Each item and subitem should have a `[ ]` checkbox"), so the author's choice is defensible; either way the markers sit at correct, tested points (after each section's tests pass) rather than after every task or only at the end. No action required.

findings.title: Task 5.2 directs editing the completed slice design retroactively
findings.description: The trailing note in Task 5.2 instructs: "Update the slice design's Verification Walkthrough with any actual command output, corrections, or caveats discovered during implementation." No success criterion requires this, and mutating a completed design document during implementation risks diverging the design record from what was reviewed. If the walkthrough turns out to be wrong, a note in the commit message or a follow-up issue would keep the design doc stable. Minor, since the walkthrough looks accurate as written.

findings.title: Some step-level detail exceeds what the slice strictly requires
findings.description: Task 2.3 enumerates ~16 individually named unit tests with exact coordinates, and Task 3.3 dictates the exact log-line format (`%s` with `.value`). The slice requires coverage categories (edge-exact, single/large/negative overshoot, passthrough) rather than a named test list, so this is over-specification in the strict sense. That said, each enumerated test maps to a stated coverage category, the coordinates make the tests mechanical for a junior implementer, and the total test count is proportionate to a vectorized numpy module with well-defined edge semantics. Similarly, splitting the new ~50-line enforcement module across Tasks 2.1 and 2.2 is slightly granular but each task is independently verifiable. Nothing here needs cutting; flagging only for transparency.
